name: Pomegranate
summary: Its juice is rich in tannins called punicalagins. In small trials, drinking 100% pomegranate juice lowered blood pressure by about 5 mmHg; its other effects are mixed or unclear.
inIt: Pomegranate is known for ellagitannins, a kind of tannin. The main one is punicalagin. In one study, 180 mL of pomegranate juice held 318 mg of ellagitannins (as punicalagins) and 25 mg of ellagic acid.
Juices also contain anthocyanins (the red colour), ellagic acid compounds and other tannins, measured in commercial and home-pressed juices in a 2000 study.

The UK food table (CoFID) measures the basic nutrients in the seeds: per 100 g, 51 kcal, 11.8 g of sugars, 13 mg of vitamin C and 240 mg of potassium. It has no fibre value for them, and it measures none of the ellagitannins, anthocyanins or other polyphenols.
The body takes up little of these compounds as they are. After juice, ellagic acid showed up in the blood within about an hour and was gone by about four hours.

Gut bacteria turn ellagic acid into urolithins, which stay in the body longer. People differ a lot: in intervention trials, 25 to 80% of people made only urolithin A, 10 to 50% also made other urolithins, and 5 to 25% made none that could be detected. In a group of 839 people, age was the main factor linked to which type someone was.
Nobody knows yet which of these compounds, if any, explains the effects seen in trials. A food has thousands of compounds that food tables don't track.

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Pliny the Elder, Natural History, about AD 77)
lore.belief: Pliny wrote that sweet pomegranates were generally thought bad for the stomach, gave people wind and harmed the teeth and gums, while the 'vinous' kind was more wholesome and, eaten in moderation rather than to the full, settled the stomach and bowels. No kind, he said, should be given to people with a fever, or to people who were vomiting.
lore.note: No study on this page looked at what pomegranate does to the teeth, gums or stomach, or at people with a fever. The trials measured blood pressure, blood fats, blood sugar and similar markers.

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Pliny the Elder, Natural History, about AD 77)
lore.belief: Pliny reported that doctors called pomegranate rind a diuretic (it makes people pass more water), that the rind boiled with oak galls in vinegar was said to firm up loose teeth in their sockets, and that it was given to pregnant women troubled by queasiness.
lore.note: Nobody has tested pomegranate rind for loose teeth, passing water or nausea in pregnancy. The studies on this page used the juice or the fruit; rind and peel extracts are a different intervention.

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Pliny the Elder, Natural History, about AD 77)
lore.belief: Pliny described 'stomatice', the juice of sour pomegranates boiled down to a third and mixed with saffron, alum, myrrh and honey, as extremely good for sores of the mouth, nostrils and ears, for dimness of sight and films over the eyes, and for diseases of the genitals.
lore.note: No study on this page has tested pomegranate juice for mouth, ear or eye complaints, and a mixture with alum and myrrh would be a different remedy from the fruit.

lore.who: Chinese medicine (the Mingyi Bielu and later physicians, quoted by Li Shizhen in 1578)
lore.belief: Chinese physicians wrote that sweet pomegranates eased a dry, parched throat and thirst, but warned that eating many harmed the lungs and, Meng Shen added, turned the teeth black. Zhu Zhenheng thought the sour, sluggish juice clung inside the chest and made phlegm.
lore.note: No study on this page has tested pomegranate for thirst or a dry throat, or looked for harm to the lungs or teeth. Pliny, writing in Rome, had also thought sweet pomegranates bad for the teeth.

lore.who: Ancient Greece (Homeric Hymn to Demeter, about 600 BC)
lore.belief: The Greeks told how Hades carried Persephone off to the underworld and, before letting her go home, secretly gave her a pomegranate seed to eat. Because she had tasted food there, she had to go back to him for a third of every year; when she returned to her mother Demeter in spring, the earth bloomed again.
lore.note: Here the pomegranate is the food of the dead, the thing that binds Persephone to the underworld; a 2000 history in the BMJ reads it as a symbol of life, renewal and marriage. No ancient text or scholarly source found for this page calls the pomegranate ambrosia (the food that kept the Greek gods immortal) or 'the closest thing to ambrosia'.

lore.belief: Pomegranates of blue, purple and crimson yarn hung between golden bells on the hem of the high priest's robe, and 200 bronze pomegranates ringed each capital of the pillars of Solomon's Temple. The spies Moses sent into Canaan brought back pomegranates with grapes and figs. The Talmud says that even the emptiest of Israel are as full of good deeds as a pomegranate is of seeds, and that dreaming of pomegranates means business will multiply like their seeds. On the eve of the New Year some eat pomegranates and pray that their merits be as many as its seeds.
lore.note: The popular saying that every pomegranate has exactly 613 seeds, one for each commandment of the Torah, is reported in modern writing (the BMJ history says it is 'said to'), but it isn't in these texts.

lore.who: Ancient Persia (Achaemenid kings, 5th century BC; Zoroastrian tradition)
lore.belief: The pomegranate was a royal emblem in Persia. Herodotus describes Xerxes' army marching with a thousand spearmen carrying golden pomegranates on their spear shafts and nine thousand with silver ones, and the reliefs at Persepolis show the fruit on the king's parasol. Zoroastrians planted pomegranate trees in the courtyards of fire temples, used its twigs and seeds in rituals, and linked it with Anahita, goddess of water and fertility. A Persian legend tells that the hero Esfandiyar ate a pomegranate and became invincible.
lore.note: Nobody has tested whether pomegranate makes people stronger; the nearest trials, on muscle soreness and damage after hard exercise, found no clear effect. A 2023 study of the Persian reliefs links immortality with the haoma drink, the date palm and myrtle, not with the pomegranate.

lore.belief: The Qur'an names pomegranates, with fruit and date palms, among the riches of the two gardens of Paradise, and on earth among God's gifts with grapevines and olives, 'similar yet varied'. A later legend says every pomegranate holds one seed that came down from Paradise.
lore.note: The legend of the seed from Paradise isn't in the Qur'an; the BMJ history reports it as a legend.

lore.belief: Hariti was a demoness who devoured children until the Buddha cured her of it, and in the legend he gave her a pomegranate to eat. She is shown holding a child, and in Japan, as Kishimojin, women who could not have children prayed to her. In Buddhist art the pomegranate is one of three blessed fruits, with the citrus and the peach.
lore.note: No study found for this page has tested whether eating pomegranate helps people have children.

lore.who: China (Northern Qi court, 6th century; a Daoist legend)
lore.belief: At a feast for a newly married prince, the bride's mother set two pomegranates before the emperor. Nobody knew why until the scholar Wei Shou explained: the pomegranate has many seeds in its chambers, and the mother was wishing the couple many children and grandchildren. The emperor, delighted, rewarded him. A Daoist tale tells of Liu Feng, who regularly took a substance called 'stone cassia flower' and pomegranates from the Central Peak, and at nearly 400 years old looked like a boy of 15.
lore.note: Both stories are quoted in the Taiping Yulan, an encyclopedia finished in 983, from the History of the Northern Dynasties and the Biographies of Divine Immortals. A picture of a split-open pomegranate became a popular wedding gift in China. Liu Feng's is the only long-life story about pomegranate found for this page, and no study has measured whether eating pomegranate lengthens human life.

lore.belief: In Christian art the pomegranate stood for the resurrection and eternal life, and it often appears in statues and paintings of the Virgin and Child. In medieval unicorn tapestries the captured unicorn is chained to a pomegranate tree, a sign of Christ's coming, and the red 'wounds' on its white body are pomegranate juice dripping from the fruit.
lore.note: The pomegranate was also the badge of Catherine of Aragon, and by the mid-1500s it was in the coat of arms of the Royal College of Physicians of London; the British Medical Association and other colleges still carry it.

history.use: The root of the pomegranate tree against tapeworms
history.note: This used the root, not the fruit, and the root is a different and riskier medicine: its alkaloids, such as pelletierine, resemble strychnine in structure, and isopelletierine is moderately toxic (in rodents, about 70 mg per kg by mouth kills half of them). A 2026 laboratory study called the evidence that these alkaloids kill worms controversial and thin, and no trial in people was found for this page.

tableFoods.label: Seeds from half a pomegranate (about 80 g)

processing: Fresh seeds (arils) and 100% juice are not the same food. In a 2000 study, commercial juices pressed from whole pomegranates held 1,500 to 1,900 mg of punicalagin per litre, while juice pressed in the lab from the seeds alone had only traces. The authors concluded that industrial pressing pulls tannins out of the rind.
Pressing with the peel made juice bitter and astringent, with more total polyphenols but fewer anthocyanins, in a 2013 study.

Many trials used 100% pomegranate juice (some of the Wonderful variety) or juice concentrate. Many others used extracts in capsules or liquid, or seed oil: those are different products, and this page keeps them apart where the studies allow.
In 16 volunteers, a cup of juice and two pomegranate extracts gave similar blood levels of ellagic acid and similar urolithin A in urine. That doesn't show they have the same effects.
The UK food table has only a sweetened pomegranate juice drink (CoFID 14-341), not pure juice, so its numbers don't describe 100% juice. It lists 0 g of fibre for that drink.
whatStudiesDid: Most trials gave 100% pomegranate juice every day for a few weeks to about 18 months. Amounts were usually around a cup (about 240 mL); meta-analyses grouped trials by up to or more than 240 mL a day, or up to or more than 300 mL a day. A trial in adults at moderate heart risk gave 240 mL a day for up to 18 months. A prostate cancer trial gave 8 ounces (about 240 mL) a day, with 570 mg of polyphenols. A trial in people on dialysis gave 100 mL at each dialysis session, three times a week, for a year. Exercise trials gave juice for a few days around hard exercise, for example 250 mL twice a day for nine days. Very few trials used the fresh seeds.

findings.population: Adults in small randomised trials, many with high blood pressure or heart risk; the 2017 and 2023 meta-analyses included 100% pomegranate juice only
whyThisGrade: Mostly small, short trials: 14 juice trials with 573 people in total in the 2023 meta-analysis
Very mixed results between trials: in the 2024 meta-analysis of all pomegranate products, heterogeneity (I²) was 90% for systolic pressure
A 2017 systematic review of 8 trials judged the evidence weak: only 2 found a clear fall in systolic pressure
In the 2023 meta-analysis the effect was seen in trials of up to 2 months and not in longer ones
The abstracts don't say who funded most trials
findings.summary: A 2017 meta-analysis of 8 randomised placebo-controlled trials of pomegranate juice found systolic blood pressure 4.96 mmHg lower (95% confidence interval 2.25 to 7.67 lower) and diastolic 2.01 mmHg lower (0.31 to 3.71 lower). A 2023 meta-analysis of 14 juice trials (573 people) found systolic pressure 5.02 mmHg lower (2.48 to 7.55 lower). In trials with up to 300 mL a day it was 6.11 mmHg lower; with more than 300 mL a day, 3.28 mmHg lower, which could be chance. Trials of up to 2 months found a fall, and the authors wrote that the benefit was lost after 2 months. A 2024 meta-analysis of 22 trials of all pomegranate products (juice, extracts and others mixed) found systolic 7.87 and diastolic 3.23 mmHg lower, with a larger fall when systolic pressure started above 130 mmHg, but results varied widely between trials. A 2017 systematic review of 8 trials, rating their reporting, concluded that the trials did not convincingly show a benefit and called for longer, better trials. No trial measured heart attacks or strokes.
findings.bottomLine: In meta-analyses of small trials, drinking pomegranate juice went with systolic blood pressure about 5 mmHg lower and diastolic about 2 mmHg lower. Trials were short and results varied a lot, the fall wasn't seen in trials longer than 2 months, and one review called the evidence weak.
findings.label: Blood pressure
findings.line: About 5 mmHg lower (top number) in short juice trials; not seen past 2 months

findings.outcome: Blood fats (LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides)
findings.population: Adults in small randomised trials, healthy or with metabolic problems such as diabetes or fatty liver
whyThisGrade: Meta-analyses disagree: two found no effect on blood fats, a newer one of juice alone found small changes
A 2020 review rated the certainty of the evidence as low (GRADE), because results were imprecise and inconsistent
The juice-only meta-analysis found high heterogeneity and many trials did not describe how people were randomised
The changes found are small: a few mg/dL
findings.summary: A 2026 meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials of pomegranate juice only (663 people; full text read) found triglycerides 8.2 mg/dL lower (95% confidence interval 0.12 to 16.3 lower), LDL cholesterol 4.8 mg/dL lower (0.16 to 9.4 lower) and HDL cholesterol 2.8 mg/dL higher (0.9 to 4.72 higher), with no change in total cholesterol; results varied a lot between trials, and the changes looked larger in people with metabolic disorders. Older meta-analyses did not find this: a 2016 meta-analysis of 12 trials (545 people) found no effect of pomegranate on any blood fat, and a 2020 review of 17 trials (763 people) found no effect and rated the evidence low. A 2025 meta-analysis of 37 trials of juice, extracts and seed oil together (2,695 people) found HDL 2.5 mg/dL higher and no change in total cholesterol, LDL or triglycerides.
findings.bottomLine: Results disagree. The newest meta-analysis of pomegranate juice alone found slightly lower LDL and triglycerides and slightly higher HDL, a few mg/dL each, but earlier meta-analyses found no effect and one rated the evidence low.
findings.label: Cholesterol and triglycerides
findings.line: Results disagree: the newest review found small improvements, earlier ones none

findings.population: Adults in randomised trials, many in Iran, including people with type 2 diabetes or polycystic ovary syndrome
whyThisGrade: Two meta-analyses of juice disagree: the first found no clear effect, the update found a much larger fall
The update's effect came mainly from some subgroups (Iranian trials, type 2 diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome)
Small trials; CRP is a marker in the blood, not an illness
The certainty rating of the 2024 update isn't given in its abstract
findings.summary: A 2016 meta-analysis of 5 randomised trials of pomegranate juice (427 people) found no clear effect on CRP (0.22 mg/L lower, 95% confidence interval 0.45 lower to 0.01 higher). A 2024 update with 11 juice trials (696 people) found CRP 2.55 mg/L lower (1.66 to 3.44 lower), with the fall seen in subgroups such as Iranian trials, people with type 2 diabetes or polycystic ovary syndrome, and trials with less than 250 mL a day; it found no link with dose or duration. A 2023 meta-analysis of 33 trials of all pomegranate products found CRP 0.50 mg/L lower (0.20 to 0.79 lower), with lower IL-6 and TNF-α, two other inflammation markers. The two juice meta-analyses differ more than tenfold in size of effect.
findings.bottomLine: One meta-analysis of pomegranate juice found no clear effect on CRP, an inflammation marker; a later one with more trials found a fall of 2.55 mg/L, mainly in some groups such as people with type 2 diabetes. The results disagree, so the effect is uncertain.
findings.label: Inflammation (CRP)
findings.line: Results disagree between reviews of juice trials

findings.outcome: Blood sugar: fasting glucose and HbA1c (long-term blood sugar)
findings.population: Adults in randomised trials, healthy or with type 2 diabetes or metabolic syndrome
whyThisGrade: The 2025 meta-analysis rated its pooled results for all pomegranate products as moderate certainty (GRADE), but did not rate juice on its own
In juice trials, results varied very widely (heterogeneity I² 93% for fasting glucose)

findings.summary: A 2025 meta-analysis of 34 randomised trials (1,500 people; full text read) found fasting glucose 3.0 mg/dL (about 0.17 mmol/L) lower with pomegranate products of any kind, and rated this moderate certainty, but HbA1c did not change. In the 22 trials of juice, fasting glucose was 2.76 mg/dL lower (95% confidence interval 0.68 to 4.83 lower), with very mixed results between trials; insulin did not change clearly (0.29 lower, 0.74 lower to 0.17 higher) and nor did HbA1c in the 3 juice trials that measured it (0.15 percentage points lower, 0.39 lower to 0.10 higher). The one trial of the fruit itself found no change (1.30 mg/dL higher, 3.11 lower to 5.71 higher). A 2017 meta-analysis of 16 trials (538 people) found no effect on fasting glucose, insulin or HbA1c.
findings.bottomLine: In trials of pomegranate juice, fasting blood sugar was on average about 3 mg/dL (0.15 mmol/L) lower, a small change, with very mixed results; long-term blood sugar (HbA1c) did not change, and an earlier meta-analysis found no effect at all.
findings.label: Blood sugar
findings.line: Fasting sugar slightly lower, about 3 mg/dL, with very mixed results; HbA1c unchanged

findings.outcome: Thickening of the neck arteries (carotid intima-media thickness)
findings.population: Adults at moderate heart risk (randomised trial); a few people with narrowed neck arteries (small study without randomisation)
whyThisGrade: The larger, randomised trial (289 people, 18 months) found no overall difference
The study that found less thickening had 10 people drinking juice, was not randomised, and was not blinded
Artery thickness is a sign of hardening arteries, not an illness itself
The benefits in some subgroups of the larger trial were exploratory analyses
findings.summary: In a 2004 study without randomisation, 10 people with narrowed neck arteries drank pomegranate juice for a year (5 for up to 3 years). Their artery wall thickness fell by up to 30% after a year, while it rose by 9% in a control group that didn't drink juice; systolic blood pressure was 12% lower after a year and didn't fall further. A later double-blind randomised trial in 289 men and women at moderate heart risk gave 240 mL of juice a day or a control drink for up to 18 months and found no difference in how fast artery walls thickened overall. In exploratory analyses, people with the most unfavourable blood fats or oxidation markers at the start had less thickening with juice; these subgroup findings need testing.
findings.bottomLine: A very small early study without randomisation found thinner artery walls after a year of pomegranate juice. A larger randomised trial in 289 people at moderate heart risk, 240 mL a day for up to 18 months, found no overall difference.
findings.label: Neck artery thickening
findings.line: No overall difference in a randomised trial of 289 people over 18 months

findings.outcome: Prostate cancer: how fast PSA rises after treatment (PSA doubling time)
findings.population: Men whose PSA was rising again after surgery or radiotherapy for prostate cancer, and men on active surveillance
whyThisGrade: The first juice trial had no comparison group; PSA doubling time also lengthened with placebo in the later trial
In the placebo-controlled trial most men had an extract; the juice group was 17 men
PSA doubling time is a marker, not survival or spread of cancer
The benefit seen in men with one gene type (MnSOD AA) was found in an extract group and needs testing
findings.summary: In a 2006 trial without a comparison group, men with rising PSA after prostate cancer treatment drank 8 ounces (about 240 mL) of pomegranate juice a day; the average time for PSA to double rose from 15 to 54 months. A later double-blind placebo-controlled trial (183 men) mostly tested an extract: median PSA doubling time lengthened from 11.1 to 15.6 months with placebo, 12.9 to 14.5 with extract and 12.7 to 20.3 with juice (17 men), and none of these differed clearly from each other. A 2017 review concluded that pomegranate juice and extract are safe but did not clearly improve outcomes in these men in the large placebo-controlled trial. A 2021 trial of extract in 30 men on active surveillance found no difference in PSA doubling time.
findings.bottomLine: An early trial without a comparison group found PSA rising more slowly in men drinking pomegranate juice after prostate cancer treatment, but in a later placebo-controlled trial PSA slowed with placebo too, and juice or extract did not differ clearly from it.
findings.label: PSA after prostate cancer
findings.line: PSA rise not clearly slower than with placebo in a controlled trial

findings.outcome: Muscle damage and soreness after hard exercise
findings.population: Mostly young men, trained or untrained, in small trials of eccentric exercise, weightlifting or jumping
whyThisGrade: Ten small studies in the meta-analysis, mixing juice and extracts
Almost all participants were men
Different exercises, amounts and timings make trials hard to compare
Some single trials found benefits, others found none
findings.summary: A 2025 meta-analysis of 10 studies of pomegranate juice or extract found no clear effect on creatine kinase (a muscle damage marker), myoglobin, lactate or muscle soreness after hard exercise. Lactate dehydrogenase, another damage marker, was 21 U/L lower right after exercise (3.0 to 39.3 lower). Single trials of juice differ: in 17 resistance-trained men, juice went with better strength and less soreness in the arm, but not the thigh; in 36 untrained men drinking 250 mL twice a day for nine days, juice was no better than a placebo drink; and in 14 volleyball players drinking 1,000 mL around a jumping test, juice did not beat placebo on average.
findings.bottomLine: A meta-analysis of 10 small studies, mostly in young men, found no clear effect of pomegranate juice or extract on muscle soreness or most muscle damage markers after hard exercise. Single trials disagree.
findings.label: Muscle soreness after exercise
findings.line: No clear change in a review of 10 small studies

visuals.title: From pomegranate tannins to urolithins
visuals.caption: What studies of people drinking pomegranate juice found happens to its main polyphenols. How much someone makes of each urolithin depends on their gut bacteria, so the same juice may act differently in different people; whether that changes its effects is not known.

steps.label: In the juice
steps.text: In one study, 180 mL of juice held 318 mg of ellagitannins (as punicalagins) and 25 mg of ellagic acid.

steps.label: Ellagic acid in the blood
steps.text: After 180 mL of juice concentrate, ellagic acid appeared in the blood of all 18 volunteers, peaking about an hour later. In another study it was gone by 4 hours.

steps.label: Gut bacteria make urolithins
steps.text: Bacteria in the gut turn ellagic acid into urolithins. Urolithin A was found in the urine of 11 of 18 volunteers on the day of the juice and 16 of 18 the next day.

steps.label: People differ
steps.text: In trials, 25 to 80% of people made only urolithin A, 10 to 50% also made other urolithins, and 5 to 25% made none that could be detected. Age was the main factor linked to this in 839 people.

whoShouldBeCareful.note: Two case reports describe changed blood-clotting results (INR) in people on warfarin linked to pomegranate juice: in one, the INR fell too low after a woman stopped drinking the juice. Case reports can't prove the juice was the cause. Studies in volunteers found that pomegranate juice, unlike grapefruit juice, did not change how the body cleared midazolam (broken down by the enzyme CYP3A) or flurbiprofen (CYP2C9). The evidence for an interaction is weak. If you take warfarin, talk to your doctor before changing how much pomegranate juice you drink.

The UK food table lists 240 mg of potassium per 100 g of the seeds; it has no value for pure juice. Small trials in people on dialysis gave 100 mL of juice at each dialysis session and reported it as safe and well tolerated, but that doesn't show it suits everyone with kidney disease. If you have been told to limit potassium, talk to your doctor or renal dietitian.

The UK food table lists 11.8 g of sugars per 100 g of the seeds. In trials, juice did not raise fasting blood sugar or HbA1c, but if you are managing blood sugar, talk to your doctor or dietitian about juice.

cautions: A review of 66 clinical studies found side effects reported in 11; the most common were stomach and gut problems. In case reports the most serious was an allergic reaction.
In a trial of extract capsules, diarrhoea was reported in 1.9% of men on 1 g a day and 13.5% on 3 g a day. Extracts are a different product from the fruit.
Pomegranate juice is not a treatment for high blood pressure, diabetes or prostate cancer. Anything clearly out of range in your results is worth discussing with your doctor.
unknowns: Almost no trials tested eating the fresh seeds: in a 2025 meta-analysis of 34 blood sugar trials, only one used the fruit itself. What is known is mostly about juice, which differs from the seeds (commercial juice carries tannins from the rind).
No trial has measured heart attacks, strokes, cancer or deaths. The trials measured blood pressure, blood markers and artery thickness, mostly for weeks to months.

Many trials used extracts in capsules, liquid extracts or seed oil, and some meta-analyses pool them with juice. Effects of extracts can't be taken as effects of the fruit, or the other way round. The prostate cancer trials mostly tested an extract.
Who funded most trials isn't stated in the abstracts read for this page. Several trials used juice of one commercial variety (Wonderful).
Results for blood fats, blood sugar and CRP disagree between meta-analyses, and many of the newer trials come from one country (Iran), so they may not hold elsewhere.
People differ in which urolithins their gut bacteria make from pomegranate. Whether this decides who benefits is not known.
It isn't known which compounds explain any effect. The food table measures sugars, vitamin C and potassium, but none of the polyphenols, and a food has thousands of compounds no table tracks.
